title: DSA foundations starter
notice: Synthetic pilot catalogue. Durations are estimates; completion is self-reported practice.

missions.title: Map your starting point
missions.why: Choose one consistent starting point before collecting more resources.
missions.doneWhen: Write what you know about arrays and hashing and one question you want to answer.
steps: Spend five minutes noting your current experience.
Read the starter track sequence.
Write one specific outcome for this practice block.

missions.title: Trace array lookups
missions.why: Tracing operations helps connect code to time complexity.
missions.doneWhen: Trace a linear search on [4, 1, 8, 3] and explain the worst-case number of comparisons.
steps: Search for 8 by hand.
Search for a value that is absent.
Record why the comparison count changes.

missions.title: Attempt Contains Duplicate
missions.why: A set can record what has already been seen.
missions.doneWhen: Attempt the problem and record independent or with_hint completion.
steps: Read the linked problem.
Attempt a solution for twenty minutes.
Record the approach and one edge case.

missions.title: Explain the duplicate check
missions.why: Explaining an approach exposes gaps a completed checkbox misses.
missions.doneWhen: Explain a set-based solution, its space use, and an empty-input case in your own words.
steps: Trace a duplicate appearing at the end.
Explain time and space estimates.
Note one remaining uncertainty.

missions.title: Attempt Two Sum
missions.why: A lookup table can avoid repeatedly searching for a partner.
missions.doneWhen: Attempt the linked problem and record which help you used.
steps: Describe a straightforward approach.
Try a hash-map approach.
Record one example with repeated values.

missions.title: Trace a hash-map solution
missions.why: Seeing each lookup makes the algorithm easier to reconstruct.
missions.doneWhen: Explain what the map stores and when it is updated.
steps: Use a small example of your own.
Write each lookup and insertion.
Explain why one element should not be reused accidentally.

missions.title: Revisit without your notes
missions.why: Revisiting checks recall rather than merely recognising a solution.
missions.doneWhen: Attempt the idea again and honestly record whether you needed a hint.
steps: Close previous notes.
Describe the algorithm before coding.
Compare with your previous reasoning and note one improvement.

missions.title: Attempt Binary Search
missions.why: Sorted data enables a different search strategy.
missions.doneWhen: Attempt the problem and record a boundary case.
steps: Identify the sorted-input assumption.
Trace the interval on a small list.
Attempt the linked problem.

missions.title: Check binary-search boundaries
missions.why: Boundary examples help reveal off-by-one errors.
missions.doneWhen: Trace first, last, absent, and single-element cases.
steps: Use a sorted list of five values.
Trace a value below and above the list.
Explain what terminates the search.

missions.title: Compare search choices
missions.why: A useful skill is selecting an approach for the input conditions.
missions.doneWhen: Explain when linear search, hashing, or binary search fits.
steps: Choose an approach for an unsorted one-time lookup.
Choose one for repeated lookups.
State the extra storage or preprocessing tradeoff.

missions.title: Try a transfer exercise
missions.why: Applying a pattern to a different prompt is a more useful checkpoint than XP alone.
missions.doneWhen: Attempt finding the first repeated value in a sequence; record help used.
steps: Write two example sequences.
Explain a set-based approach.
Test a sequence with no repetition.

missions.title: Review the starter checkpoint
missions.why: A completed starter should end with an honest account of what needs more practice.
missions.doneWhen: Record one approach you can explain, one you cannot yet, and your next practice focus.
steps: Review your mission outcomes.
Repeat one explanation without notes.
Record a next step without claiming interview readiness.
